meta.title: The Fizlet loop: fixed step, one shared rAF
meta.description: How Fizlet runs a frame: read, step and render phases, a fixed 60 Hz step with a catch-up cap, auto-pause, settle and an fps cap for page heroes.

ld.headline: Read. Step. Render.
ld.description: How Fizlet runs a frame: read, step and render phases, a fixed 60 Hz step with a catch-up cap, auto-pause, settle and an fps cap for page heroes.

lead: Every engine on a page shares one requestAnimationFrame. Each frame runs three phases, in order, for every system: read measures the page, step simulates at a fixed rate with no DOM at all, and render writes only what changed. That split is why a game can share a page with someone else's layout and never force a reflow in its hot loop.

body.html:
One frame

  • read · once a frame

    The only phase that may measure the page: cached geometry, input edges latched. @fzlt/core/input measures its target here, at most once a frame, and only when the pointer moved.

  • step · 0 to 4 times, dt = 1/60 s

    The simulation on plain numbers and typed arrays. No DOM reads, no DOM writes, no allocation. Things that happened go on the event ring (engine.events.emit).

  • render · once a frame, with alpha

    Change-only writes through engine.ledger. Sound, effects and the HUD read the event ring here. alpha is how far the clock is between two steps, for smooth drawing.

A fixed step
that never spirals

The step is fixed (default 1/60 s, the step option), so a game runs the same on a 30 Hz phone and a 144 Hz monitor. An accumulator collects real time and runs as many steps as fit. A slow frame runs at most maxSteps steps (default 4) and drops the rest of the time: it shows in engine.stats().dropped, and the next frame starts fresh instead of trying to catch up forever.

engine.advance(seconds) runs time by hand, with no clock at all: that is how the tests, a headless run or a server step an engine.

Pause by default

An engine pauses on its own when the tab is hidden, the page is leaving, its root is scrolled off screen or the visitor is typing in one of the host page's fields. Reduced motion is opt-in (pause: { reducedMotion: true }), since most games calm their effects instead. Paused, it asks for no frames: zero CPU. engine.paused lists why.

Settle and the fps cap
for heroes and diagrams

A page hero should cost nothing while it is still. With settle: 0.5, systems call engine.busy() in any frame where something moves; half a second after the last one, the engine sleeps: no requestAnimationFrame at all until wake(), its input or start(). Settling is not a pause: pause hooks don't run and held input stays.

fps: 30 caps an ambient loop. Since 0.19.0 it caps requestAnimationFrame itself, not just the work: between frames the engine leaves the shared clock and one timer brings it back. Measured in 0.19.0: a capped scene asks for 30 frames a second (the fizz and layers heroes), and an uncapped engine on the same page no longer drags a capped one along.

body.html:
The limits

  • 1

    requestAnimationFrame per page, however many engines run

  • 60 Hz

    the default fixed step (step: 1/60)

  • 4

    catch-up steps a frame (maxSteps), then time drops

  • 64

    events a frame on the ring (events); full means dropped and counted

Questions

What happens when a hook throws?

Only its own engine stops (paused: ["stopped"]; start() resumes) and the error goes to onError(error, engine), by default console.error. The shared clock and every other engine keep running.

Can engines start or stop each other mid-frame?

Yes. Engines may start, stop or destroy each other from inside a hook; every engine still runs once per frame on one requestAnimationFrame, and engine.remove(system) inside a hook never skips the next system.
